records.source: Τὸ λοιπόν, ἀδελφοί μου, χαίρετε ἐν κυρίῳ.
records.gloss: As for the rest, brothers of me, rejoice in Lord.
pieces: Finally, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, rejoice in the Lord.

L.1: Finally, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, rejoice in [the] Lord.

R.1: And now, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, be full of joy in the Lord.

decisions.choice: as for the rest: a turn to the next matter
alternatives: in conclusion: the letter is about to end
decisions.reason: λοιπόν marks a move on to what remains to be said; it does not promise that the end is near. Paul writes two more chapters and uses the same expression again in 4:8, where the letter really is closing. The sharp change of tone at verse 2 has led some readers to suppose that two letters were joined here, but every manuscript of Philippians has the chapter in this place.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church; 4:2 names two women in it.

decisions.choice: a command to rejoice, with the Lord as its ground
alternatives: "farewell in the Lord", the everyday goodbye
decisions.reason: χαίρετε was also how a letter said goodbye, and after "as for the rest" it could sound like one. But Paul has already called for joy in 2:18, and in 4:4 he repeats "rejoice in the Lord" with "always", which only a command can have. As in 4:4, the joy is located in the Lord, not in circumstances.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, which includes the women he names in 4:2, so the inclusive default spells that out. Traditional is one tap away.

decisions.choice: be full of joy
decisions.reason: "Rejoice" is now mostly church language; Readable says what it means, as in 4:4.

decisions.choice: And now
decisions.reason: A new reader hears "finally" as "I am about to finish", yet half the letter is still to come. Literal and Balanced keep "Finally", as in 4:8, and the meaning note explains it; Readable uses a plain word for moving on.

records.heading: No confidence in the flesh

records.source: τὰ αὐτὰ γράφειν ὑμῖν ἐμοὶ μὲν οὐκ ὀκνηρόν, ὑμῖν δὲ ἀσφαλές.
records.gloss: The same things to write to you, to me on the one hand not tiresome, for you on the other hand safe.
pieces: Writing the same things to you again is no burden to me, and for you it is a safeguard.

L.1: To write the same things to you [is] not tiresome to me, and [it is] safe for you.

R.1: I don't mind writing to you about the same things again. It will help keep you safe.

decisions.choice: things Paul has told them before, here the warning that follows
alternatives: the call to rejoice just given
what he wrote in an earlier letter
decisions.reason: Paul does not say what "the same things" are. They may be the call to joy, which runs through the letter, or warnings he had already given them; verse 18 says he had often told them about the people he describes there. The word "safe" fits a warning best, so the phrase most likely points forward to verse 2. The wording keeps it open.

decisions.choice: no bother to me; a safeguard for you
decisions.reason: ὀκνηρός describes something tiresome or irksome. ἀσφαλής means secure, giving a firm footing: repeating the warning protects them. The two halves are set side by side: for Paul it costs little, for them it gives safety.

decisions.choice: again
decisions.reason: Writing "the same things" means writing them again; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: Βλέπετε τοὺς κύνας, βλέπετε τοὺς κακοὺς ἐργάτας, βλέπετε τὴν κατατομήν.
records.gloss: Watch the dogs, watch the bad workers, watch the mutilation.
pieces: Be on guard against the dogs, be on guard against the evil workers, be on guard against the mutilators.

L.2: Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for the mutilation.

R.2: Watch out for those dogs! Watch out for those people who do evil work! Watch out for those who cut the body and call it circumcision!

decisions.choice: dogs: a name of contempt for the unclean
decisions.reason: In the ancient world dogs were mostly scavengers of the street, and Jewish speech used "dogs" as an insult for the unclean, including Gentiles (compare Matthew 15:26 and Revelation 22:15). Paul turns the insult back on people who prided themselves on Jewish marks of belonging.

decisions.choice: workers, as in workers for God, whose work does harm
decisions.reason: ἐργάτης was a word for people at work in God's service (Matthew 9:37-38; 2 Timothy 2:15). In 2 Corinthians 11:13 Paul uses it of "deceitful workers" who rivaled him. These people are busy about religion, but their work is evil.

decisions.choice: mutilation: a pun on circumcision
decisions.reason: κατατομή means a cutting up or mutilating. It rhymes with περιτομή, "circumcision", which Paul uses in the next verse. He refuses to give the name "circumcision" to what these people demand: once Christ has come, cutting the body to earn a place among God's people is mere mutilation, like the gashing of the body that the Law forbade (Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28). Compare Galatians 5:12.

decisions.choice: one group, described three ways: people who insisted that believers must be circumcised
decisions.reason: Verse 3 answers all three names at once with "we are the circumcision", so they point to one group whose message was circumcision. Whether they were believers who taught that Gentiles must keep the Law of Moses, as in Acts 15:1 and Galatians, or Jews outside the church, the letter does not say.

decisions.choice: the mutilation (L); the mutilators (B); those who cut the body and call it circumcision (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek pun cannot be copied. Literal keeps the noun, which names the act; Balanced names the people, as the other two warnings do; Readable spells out the point of the pun, which verse 3 makes plain. The meaning note gives the wordplay.

decisions.choice: be on guard against
decisions.reason: βλέπετε, said three times, is a warning to keep an eye on something dangerous. Balanced keeps the threefold repetition.

records.source: ἡμεῖς γάρ ἐσμεν ἡ περιτομή, οἱ πνεύματι θεοῦ λατρεύοντες καὶ καυχώμενοι ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ οὐκ ἐν σαρκὶ πεποιθότες, καίπερ ἐγὼ ἔχων πεποίθησιν καὶ ἐν σαρκί.
records.gloss: We for are the circumcision, the ones by Spirit of God worshiping and boasting in Christ Jesus and not in flesh having confidence, \v 4 although I having confidence also in flesh.
pieces: For it is we who are the circumcision: we who worship by the Spirit of God, who take pride in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, and who put no confidence in human credentials,
even though I myself have grounds for that kind of confidence too.

L.3: For we are the circumcision, who worship by [the] Spirit of God and boast in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus and have not put confidence in [the] flesh,
L.4: although I myself have confidence even in [the] flesh.

R.3: It is we who are truly circumcised. We worship by the power of God's Spirit. We boast about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, and we do not trust in who we are or what we have done.
R.4: Yet I myself have reasons to trust in those things.

decisions.choice: the circumcision: God's own covenant people
decisions.reason: "The circumcision" was a name for the Jewish people, marked as God's own by circumcision (Genesis 17:9-14). Paul gives the name to everyone who belongs to Christ, Gentiles included. He says the same in Romans 2:28-29 and Colossians 2:11, and the Law and the Prophets already spoke of a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: who worship by the Spirit of God
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts change the ending of the word for God, so that it reads "who worship God in spirit", and at least one early papyrus has no word for God at all. The SBLGNT follows the reading of the oldest major manuscripts. It is also the harder reading: the verb usually names the one worshiped, so copyists were more likely to supply "God" as its object than to remove it. Either way the worship is the work of the Spirit, not of the flesh.

decisions.choice: boast in, take pride in, rely on with joy
decisions.reason: καυχάομαι means to boast or exult in what one trusts. Believers make Christ their boast rather than themselves, as Jeremiah 9:23-24 says (quoted in 1 Corinthians 1:31).

decisions.choice: the flesh: human status and achievement, what a person is and does apart from God
decisions.reason: Here σάρξ means human standing as people measure it: birth, rite, rank and religious record, the very things listed in verses 5-6. The word fits because circumcision is cut in the flesh, but the point is not the body. It is trusting in oneself rather than in Christ.

decisions.choice: Paul really has these grounds, though he does not rely on them
alternatives: Paul is only supposing for the sake of argument
decisions.reason: The participle states a fact: by human standards Paul has every reason for such confidence, as verses 5-6 will show. He mentions it to show what he has given up, not because he still trusts it.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: human credentials (B); who we are or what we have done (R)
decisions.reason: In everyday English "flesh" means the body or bodily desire, which is not the sense here. Literal keeps "flesh" so the reader can trace the word through verse 4; Balanced and Readable say what it means.

decisions.choice: truly circumcised
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Paul is claiming the real meaning of circumcision for believers, which the contrast with verse 2 makes clear.

records.source: Εἴ τις δοκεῖ ἄλλος πεποιθέναι ἐν σαρκί, ἐγὼ μᾶλλον· περιτομῇ ὀκταήμερος, ἐκ γένους Ἰσραήλ, φυλῆς Βενιαμίν, Ἑβραῖος ἐξ Ἑβραίων, κατὰ νόμον Φαρισαῖος, κατὰ ζῆλος διώκων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, κατὰ δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ γενόμενος ἄμεμπτος.
records.gloss: If anyone thinks other to have confidence in flesh, I more: \v 5 in circumcision eighth-day, of race Israel, of tribe Benjamin, Hebrew of Hebrews, according to law Pharisee, \v 6 according to zeal persecuting the church, according to righteousness the in law having become blameless.
pieces: If anyone else thinks there are grounds for confidence in human credentials, I have more.
I was circumcised on the eighth day. I belong to the people of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews. In keeping the law I was a Pharisee;
in zeal I persecuted the church; in righteousness as the law defines it, I was beyond reproach.

L.4: If anyone else thinks [there is reason] to have confidence in [the] flesh, I [have] more:
L.5: circumcised [on the] eighth day, of [the] people of Israel, of [the] tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to [the] law, a Pharisee;
L.6: as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness that [is] in [the] law, having become blameless.

R.4: Some people think they can trust in who they are and what they have done. I have even more reasons to.
R.5: I was circumcised when I was eight days old, as Jewish boys are. I was born into the people of Israel, into the tribe of Benjamin. I am a Hebrew, and so were my parents. When it came to the law, I was a Pharisee, part of a group that kept it very strictly.
R.6: I was so eager to defend God's law that I attacked the church. And when it came to being righteous by keeping the law, no one could find any fault in me.

decisions.choice: verses 5-6 complete "I more"; one sentence
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has a raised dot after "I more". What follows has no verb of its own: it lists the grounds for that claim. So the record keeps verses 4b-6 together.

decisions.choice: circumcised as a Jewish baby, not as an adult convert
decisions.reason: The Law set circumcision on the eighth day after birth (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). Paul was born into the covenant; he did not join it later.

decisions.choice: of an honored tribe
decisions.reason: Benjamin gave Israel its first king, Saul, whose name Paul also bore (Acts 13:9, 21), and Paul names his tribe again in Romans 11:1.

decisions.choice: a Hebrew born of Hebrew parents
decisions.reason: The phrase means a Hebrew descended from Hebrews. It may also mean that his family kept the language and ways of their people while living abroad in Tarsus: Acts 6:1 distinguishes "Hebrews" from Greek-speaking Jews, and Acts 21:40 has Paul speaking to the crowd in the Hebrew language.

decisions.choice: a Pharisee in his approach to the law
decisions.reason: The Pharisees were a movement known for exact keeping of the law and its traditions; Paul calls them "the strictest party of our religion" in Acts 26:5.

decisions.choice: zeal for God and his law, which drove him to persecute
decisions.reason: Paul uses "zeal" of his devotion to God and the traditions of his fathers, which led him to hunt down believers (Acts 22:3-4; Galatians 1:13-14). The verb is the same one he uses for his pursuit of Christ in verses 12 and 14.

decisions.choice: measured by the law's standard, his record was beyond reproach
decisions.reason: Paul is not claiming to have been without sin. He means that by the standard the law sets, as people could see and judge it, no charge could be brought against him; the law itself provided sacrifices for failures. Verse 9 sets this "righteousness of my own" against the righteousness that comes from God.

decisions.choice: as Jewish boys are; part of a group that kept it very strictly; eager to defend God's law
decisions.reason: Readable explains facts the first readers knew: why the eighth day matters, who the Pharisees were, and what Paul's zeal was for. Each follows the meaning notes; the last draws on Acts 22:3 and Galatians 1:14.

decisions.choice: beyond reproach (B); no one could find any fault in me (R)
decisions.reason: ἄμεμπτος means that no one could lay blame; the English keeps the sense of a record others could inspect, not a claim to be sinless.

records.source: Ἀλλὰ ἅτινα ἦν μοι κέρδη, ταῦτα ἥγημαι διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν.
records.gloss: But whatever things were to me gains, these I have considered because of the Christ loss.
pieces: But whatever was profit to me, I have come to count as loss because of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.7: But whatever [things] were gains to me, these I have counted [as] loss because of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.7: But all those things I once thought were in my favor, I now see as a loss, because of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: gains and loss: the language of a business ledger
decisions.reason: κέρδος and ζημία are trading words: profit and loss. The plural "gains" (each advantage listed in verses 5-6) becomes a single "loss": taken together they have moved to the other column. The ledger image runs on through verse 8.

decisions.choice: a settled judgment, made once and still held
decisions.reason: ἥγημαι is a perfect: Paul reached this verdict in the past and it still stands. In verse 8 he switches to the present to say he holds it today.

decisions.choice: because of Christ: Christ is the reason for the new valuation
decisions.reason: διὰ with the accusative gives the reason. Knowing Christ changed the worth of everything else; verse 8 explains how.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article; Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: profit (B); in my favor (R)
decisions.reason: "Profit" keeps the ledger image in natural English; Readable says what a gain on the account means.

records.source: ἀλλὰ μενοῦνγε καὶ ἡγοῦμαι πάντα ζημίαν εἶναι διὰ τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ κυρίου μου δι’ ὃν τὰ πάντα ἐζημιώθην, καὶ ἡγοῦμαι σκύβαλα ἵνα Χριστὸν κερδήσω καὶ εὑρεθῶ ἐν αὐτῷ, μὴ ἔχων ἐμὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ νόμου ἀλλὰ τὴν διὰ πίστεως Χριστοῦ, τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει, τοῦ γνῶναι αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ καὶ κοινωνίαν παθημάτων αὐτοῦ, συμμορφιζόμενος τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ, εἴ πως καταντήσω εἰς τὴν ἐξανάστασιν τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν.
records.gloss: But more than that indeed also I consider all things loss to be because of the surpassing of the knowledge of Christ Jesus the Lord of me, because of whom the all things I suffered loss, and I consider them dung, so that Christ I may gain \v 9 and be found in him, not having my righteousness the from law but the through faith of Christ, the from God righteousness upon the faith, \v 10 the to know him and the power of the resurrection of him and sharing of sufferings of him, being conformed to the death of him, \v 11 if somehow I may arrive at the out-resurrection the from dead.
pieces: More than that, I count everything as loss because knowing {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus my Lord is worth far more than all of it. For {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sake I have lost everything, and I count it all as dung, so that I may gain {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}

and be found in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, with no righteousness of my own from keeping the law, but with the righteousness that comes through faith in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}: righteousness from God, resting on faith.

I want to know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, to know the power of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} resurrection and what it is to share in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sufferings, as I am being shaped into the likeness of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death,
hoping that somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.

L.8: But more than that, I even count all things to be loss because of the surpassing [greatness] of the knowledge of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus my Lord, because of whom I suffered the loss of all things, and I count [them] dung, so that I may gain {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
L.9: and be found in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, not having my own righteousness that [is] from [the] law, but that which [is] through faith in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the righteousness from God [resting] on faith,
L.10: to know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and the power of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} resurrection and [the] sharing of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sufferings, being conformed to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death,
L.11: if somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from [the] dead.

R.8: More than that, I count everything as a loss, because knowing {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus my Lord is worth so much more. Because of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} I have lost everything, and I think of it all as no better than dung. What I want is to gain {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
R.9: and to be found joined to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. I do not want a righteousness of my own that comes from keeping the law. I want the righteousness that comes through faith in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. That righteousness comes from God, and it is received by faith.
R.10: I want to know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and the power of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rising from death. I want to share in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sufferings and become like {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death.
R.11: Then I hope that, somehow, I too will rise from the dead.

decisions.choice: more than that: Paul goes further than verse 7
decisions.reason: The run of particles strengthens what he has just said. Verse 7 spoke of his former advantages; now he counts "all things" loss, and the present tense says he still does.

decisions.choice: the surpassing worth of knowing Christ personally
decisions.reason: γνῶσις here is knowing a person, as the Scriptures speak of knowing God (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:3), not information about him; verse 10 makes the aim "to know him". ὑπερέχω is the same verb as in 4:7, where God's peace surpasses all understanding.

decisions.choice: Paul actually lost these things, not only counted them lost
decisions.reason: ἐζημιώθην is a passive past-tense verb: he suffered the loss. Becoming a follower of Jesus cost him the standing he had described in verses 5-6.

decisions.choice: filth fit only to be thrown out; a deliberately coarse word
alternatives: rubbish, garbage: worthless but not crude
decisions.reason: σκύβαλον was used both of refuse, such as scraps thrown to the dogs, and of excrement. Either way it is the strongest word Paul could find for something worthless and repellent, and it has a coarse edge. Which of the two senses is uppermost cannot be settled; both say the same thing about the value of his old advantages.

decisions.choice: gain Christ and be found in him: belong to Christ now and when God examines his life
decisions.reason: The ledger image goes on: what now stands in the profit column is Christ himself. "Be found" looks at how God will find him; being "in him" is Paul's way of speaking of union with Christ, which is already true and will be shown at the end.

decisions.choice: righteousness as a right standing before God
decisions.reason: Here righteousness is a standing before God, not simply good conduct. Paul contrasts a righteousness "of my own", the law-measured record of verse 6, with one that comes "from God". Romans 10:3 makes the same contrast.

decisions.choice: through faith in Christ
decisions.reason: With a person's name after it, πίστις can mean faith that person has or faith directed to that person. Read the first way, Paul means Christ's own faithfulness to God, shown in his obedience to death (2:8), and "on faith" at the end of the verse is the believer's answer. Read the second way, he means the believer's faith in Christ. For "faith in Christ": the end of the verse most naturally speaks of the believer's faith, and in Galatians 2:16 the same kind of phrase sits beside "we too have believed in Christ Jesus". For "faithfulness of Christ": the verse would otherwise say the same thing twice, and Paul writes of "the faith of Abraham" for Abraham's own faith (Romans 4:16) and of "the faithfulness of God" (Romans 3:3). Both readings agree that this righteousness comes from God and not from the law. We follow the first and give the second in a footnote.

decisions.choice: resting on faith: faith is how it is received
decisions.reason: ἐπὶ gives the basis: this righteousness is God's gift and faith is the ground on which it is received, not a new achievement that earns it.

decisions.choice: to know him: the aim of everything before
decisions.reason: The article with the infinitive gives the purpose of all that precedes: gaining Christ and being found in him lead to knowing him. To know Christ is to know him in experience: his risen power and his sufferings.

decisions.choice: the power shown in Christ's resurrection, now at work in believers
alternatives: only the future resurrection of believers
decisions.reason: Paul wants to know now the power that raised Jesus, the same power God puts to work in those who believe (Romans 8:11; Ephesians 1:19-20). He speaks of his own future resurrection separately, in verse 11.

decisions.choice: a sharing, a partnership in his sufferings
decisions.reason: κοινωνία is a key word in this letter: partnership in the gospel (1:5) and sharing in the Spirit (2:1). Here Paul shares in what Christ suffered, as he does in his imprisonment (1:29-30).

decisions.choice: being shaped to match his death: an echo of 2:6-8
decisions.reason: συμμορφίζομαι is built on the word for "form" used in 2:6-7, where Christ, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant and was obedient to death. The present tense says it is happening now. Verse 21 completes the pattern: the one being shaped to his death will be given a body shaped like his glory.

decisions.choice: humble hope, not doubt that God will raise him
alternatives: real uncertainty about his own salvation
decisions.reason: εἴ πως, "if somehow", expresses hope and humility about the way ahead, perhaps through death or martyrdom, rather than doubt about the outcome; elsewhere in the letter Paul is sure that dying means being with Christ (1:21-23) and that Christ will transform his body (3:21). Verses 12-14 show the same humility: he has not yet arrived.

decisions.choice: the resurrection out from among the dead
decisions.reason: ἐξανάστασις occurs only here in the New Testament. Its extra prefix, with "from the dead", points to rising out from among those who have died: the resurrection of those who belong to Christ.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}
decisions.reason: Pronouns for Christ follow the reader's setting.

decisions.choice: dung (L, B); no better than dung (R)
decisions.reason: The word is harsher than "rubbish" or "garbage", which make Paul sound merely tidy. "Dung" keeps both the worthlessness and the coarse edge without being vulgar to a modern ear. A footnote gives the milder "rubbish".

decisions.choice: three English sentences; "I want to know him"; "hoping"
decisions.reason: Balanced breaks Paul's long sentence after "faith" and starts again with "I want to know him", which states the purpose the infinitive gives. "Hoping" carries the "if somehow" of verse 11 (meaning note m13).

decisions.choice: joined to him; from keeping the law; received by faith; I hope
decisions.reason: Readable says what each short phrase means: being "in" Christ is being joined to him (as in 4:7), righteousness "from the law" is the kind earned by keeping it, "on faith" means faith is how it is received, and "if somehow" expresses hope.

records.source: Οὐχ ὅτι ἤδη ἔλαβον ἢ ἤδη τετελείωμαι, διώκω δὲ εἰ καὶ καταλάβω, ἐφ’ ᾧ καὶ κατελήμφθην ὑπὸ Χριστοῦ.
records.gloss: Not that already I received or already have been perfected, I pursue but if also I may lay hold, on which also I was laid hold of by Christ.
pieces: I do not mean that I already have all this, or that I have already been made perfect. But I keep pursuing it, trying to take hold of it, because {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has taken hold of me.

L.12: Not that I have already received [it] or have already been made perfect, but I pursue [it], if indeed I may lay hold [of it], because I also was laid hold of by {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.12: I am not saying that I already have all this, or that I am already perfect. But I keep running after it, trying to catch hold of it, because {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} caught hold of me.

decisions.choice: what he has not yet received: the goal of verses 10-11
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. The context supplies it: full knowledge of Christ and the resurrection Paul has just spoken of. He guards against anyone thinking he has already arrived.

decisions.choice: brought to completion, made perfect
decisions.reason: τελειόω means to bring something to its goal or finish. Paul says he has not yet reached that end. In verse 15 he plays on the related word for "mature".

decisions.choice: pursue, chase: the same verb as "persecuting" in verse 6
decisions.reason: διώκω means to run after, whether to catch someone or to reach a goal. The man who once pursued the church now pursues Christ. Verses 13-14 develop it as a runner's race.

decisions.choice: because
decisions.reason: ἐφ’ ᾧ can mean "because" or "that for which". Paul uses the phrase to mean "because" in Romans 5:12, 2 Corinthians 5:4 and Philippians 4:10, and that fits here: Christ took hold of him first. Read the other way, Paul pursues the purpose for which Christ took hold of him. The two are close; the footnote gives the other.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: by Christ
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "Jesus". The meaning does not change, so there is no footnote.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: lay hold / laid hold (L); take hold / taken hold (B); catch hold / caught hold (R)
decisions.reason: Paul uses the same verb twice, once active and once passive. Every level repeats the English verb so the reader sees the play: he reaches for what Christ has already reached him for.

records.heading: Running for the goal

records.source: ἀδελφοί, ἐγὼ ἐμαυτὸν οὐ λογίζομαι κατειληφέναι· ἓν δέ, τὰ μὲν ὀπίσω ἐπιλανθανόμενος τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος, κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω εἰς τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: Brothers, I myself not consider to have laid hold; one thing but, the things on the one hand behind forgetting, to the things on the other hand ahead stretching out, \v 14 toward goal I pursue to the prize of the upward calling of the God in Christ Jesus.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I do not count myself as having taken hold of it. My single aim is this: I put out of mind what is behind me and stretch out for what is in front of me,
and I run straight for the goal to win the prize promised by God's upward call in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.13: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I do not consider myself to have laid hold [of it]; but one thing [I do]: forgetting the things behind and stretching out to the things ahead,
L.14: I pursue toward [the] goal, for the prize of the upward call of God in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.13: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I do not think I have caught hold of it yet. But I do one thing. I forget what is behind me and reach out for what is ahead.
R.14: I run straight for the finish line to win the prize God holds out to me when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} calls me up to heaven through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church; 4:2 names two women in it.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: not
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "not yet". After "already" in verse 12 the sense is the same, so there is no footnote.

decisions.choice: one thing: a single focus, with no verb
decisions.reason: Paul writes only "but one thing"; the verb is left out for force, and the rest of the sentence says what that one thing is.

decisions.choice: no longer letting the past count or hold him back
decisions.reason: Paul has just recalled his past in detail (verses 4-6), so he does not mean he cannot remember it. Like a runner who does not look back, he no longer relies on it or lets it hold him.

decisions.choice: a footrace: straining forward, running for the mark, the winner's prize
decisions.reason: ἐπεκτείνομαι pictures a runner stretching toward the line; σκοπός is the mark the eye is fixed on; βραβεῖον is the prize for winning a race, as in 1 Corinthians 9:24.

decisions.choice: the prize that God's call upward holds out
alternatives: the call itself is the prize
the call to come up and receive the prize
decisions.reason: God calls his people upward, to the life above where Christ is (compare Colossians 3:1-2), and the prize is what that call promises. The phrase can also be read with the call itself as the prize, or as the summons that brings the winner up to receive it. All three readings agree that God is the one who calls and the goal is above.

decisions.choice: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, which includes the women he names in 4:2, so the inclusive default spells that out. Traditional is one tap away.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: finish line; calls me up to heaven; through
decisions.reason: Readable names the race picture and says where "upward" leads. "Yet" follows from "already" in verse 12.

records.source: ὅσοι οὖν τέλειοι, τοῦτο φρονῶμεν· καὶ εἴ τι ἑτέρως φρονεῖτε, καὶ τοῦτο ὁ θεὸς ὑμῖν ἀποκαλύψει·
records.gloss: As many as therefore mature, this let us think; and if anything differently you think, also this the God to you will reveal.
pieces: Those of us, then, who are mature should have this mindset. And if your thinking differs at some point, God will reveal that to you as well.

L.15: As many as [are] perfect, therefore, let us think this; and if in anything you think differently, God will reveal this also to you.

R.15: All of us who are grown up as believers should think this way. If you think differently about something, God will make that clear to you too.

decisions.choice: mature, full-grown; with a play on "made perfect" in verse 12
decisions.reason: τέλειος means complete or full-grown, and is related to the verb in verse 12. Paul has just said he is not yet "made perfect"; now he calls the "mature" to share his view. Being mature means knowing you have not arrived. He may also be turning a word some in Philippi used of themselves.

decisions.choice: this way of thinking: the outlook of verses 7-14
decisions.reason: φρονέω is the letter's word for a whole mindset (2:2, 2:5, 4:2). "This" is the outlook Paul has just described: counting everything loss for Christ and pressing on.

decisions.choice: on some point of difference, God will make the truth plain
alternatives: a promise that every opinion is right
decisions.reason: Paul expects God to correct and lead them on matters where they still see things differently; he leaves that to God rather than forcing it.

decisions.choice: perfect (L); mature (B); grown up as believers (R)
decisions.reason: Literal says "perfect" so the reader can see the play on verse 12. Balanced and Readable give the sense, since "perfect" in modern English would contradict verse 12; the footnote gives "perfect".

records.source: πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχεῖν.
records.gloss: Only, to what we have attained, by the same to keep in line.
pieces: In any case, let us keep in step with the point we have already reached.

L.16: Only, to what we have attained, [let us] keep in line by the same.

R.16: Anyway, let us keep walking in step with how far we have already come.

decisions.choice: keep in line, walk in step
decisions.reason: στοιχέω is to walk in a row or keep in line, as soldiers do; Paul uses it in Galatians 5:25 for keeping in step with the Spirit.

decisions.choice: a call that includes Paul: let us keep to it
decisions.reason: The infinitive stands for a command, and "we have attained" includes Paul with them. Whatever still differs (verse 15), they should not fall back from the ground already gained.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: the shorter text
alternatives: adds "by the same rule, let us think the same thing"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add words meaning "rule" and "let us think the same thing", and the King James Version follows them. The earliest manuscripts have the short text; the addition seems to borrow from Galatians 6:16 and Philippians 2:2.

decisions.choice: [let us]
decisions.reason: English cannot use a bare infinitive as a command; Literal supplies "let us" in brackets, matching "we".

records.source: Συμμιμηταί μου γίνεσθε, ἀδελφοί, καὶ σκοπεῖτε τοὺς οὕτω περιπατοῦντας καθὼς ἔχετε τύπον ἡμᾶς·
records.gloss: Fellow-imitators of me become, brothers, and watch the ones so walking, just as you have pattern us.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, all of you together, follow my example, and take note of those who live this way, by the pattern you have in us.

L.17: Become fellow imitators of me, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, and watch those who walk this way, just as you have us [as] a pattern.

R.17: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, all of you should follow my example together. Pay attention to the people who live the way we do. We have shown you how.

decisions.choice: join with one another in imitating me
alternatives: imitate me, as I imitate Christ, alongside me
decisions.reason: συμμιμητής occurs only here. Its first part means "together": the church as a body is to follow Paul's example, the example of counting all things loss for Christ (verses 7-14). Compare 1 Corinthians 11:1 and 4:9 in this letter.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church; 4:2 names two women in it.

decisions.choice: walk: live, conduct one's life
decisions.reason: To "walk" is a biblical way of speaking of how one lives (Psalm 1:1; Romans 6:4). Verse 18 uses the same verb for those who live otherwise.

decisions.choice: "us": Paul and co-workers such as Timothy and Epaphroditus
decisions.reason: Paul switches from "me" to "us". He has just held up Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples (2:19-30). σκοπεῖτε, "watch", is related to the "goal" of verse 14: they are to fix their eyes on such people.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, which includes the women he names in 4:2, so the inclusive default spells that out. Traditional is one tap away.

decisions.choice: live
decisions.reason: "Walk" in this sense is not current English; Literal keeps it.

records.source: πολλοὶ γὰρ περιπατοῦσιν οὓς πολλάκις ἔλεγον ὑμῖν, νῦν δὲ καὶ κλαίων λέγω, τοὺς ἐχθροὺς τοῦ σταυροῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὧν τὸ τέλος ἀπώλεια, ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία καὶ ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ αἰσχύνῃ αὐτῶν, οἱ τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονοῦντες.
records.gloss: Many for walk, whom often I was telling you, now but even weeping I say, the enemies of the cross of the Christ, \v 19 of whom the end destruction, of whom the god the belly and the glory in the shame of them, the ones the earthly things thinking.
pieces: For many live as enemies of the cross of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. I have often told you about them, and now I tell you again, in tears.
Destruction is where they will end. The belly is their god, they find their glory in what should make them ashamed, and earthly things fill their minds.

L.18: For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now I tell [you] even weeping, [as] the enemies of the cross of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}},
L.19: whose end [is] destruction, whose god [is] the belly, and [whose] glory [is] in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things.

R.18: I have told you many times before, and now I tell you again with tears: many people are living as enemies of the cross of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
R.19: In the end they will be destroyed. Their real god is their own appetite. They find glory in things they should be ashamed of. All they think about is the things of this world.

decisions.choice: enemies of the cross by the way they live
decisions.reason: "Walk" again means how they live (verse 17). The cross stands for Christ's self-giving death (2:8), the pattern Paul is being shaped by (3:10). These people may well claim to follow Christ, but their way of life opposes what the cross means.

decisions.choice: grief, not contempt
decisions.reason: Paul says he is weeping as he writes. The warning comes from sorrow for them.

decisions.choice: their end is final ruin
decisions.reason: τέλος here is the outcome. ἀπώλεια is the word Paul used in 1:28 for the destruction awaiting those who oppose the gospel, the opposite of salvation; verse 20 turns to the Savior.

decisions.choice: the belly: their appetites and desires
decisions.reason: κοιλία, the belly, stands for appetite. Romans 16:18 speaks of people who serve "their own belly" rather than Christ. Some read it instead as zeal for food laws, and "shame" in the next phrase as a reference to circumcision, which would tie these people to verse 2. Nothing in this verse ties them to verse 2, and "earthly things" fits self-indulgence, so we follow that reading and footnote the other.

decisions.choice: they pride themselves on what is really their disgrace
alternatives: their glory will be turned to shame at the judgment
decisions.reason: Their "glory", what they boast of, lies in things that ought to shame them. Hosea 4:7 speaks of God turning a people's glory into shame, and that judgment may be in view as well.

decisions.choice: a mindset fixed on earthly things
decisions.reason: φρονέω again (2:5; 3:15): their whole outlook is bounded by this world, the opposite of the heavenly citizenship in verse 20.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: the belly (L, B); their own appetite (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the blunt image; Readable says what it stands for, following the meaning note.

decisions.choice: "I have told you" first
decisions.reason: Readable puts Paul's words about warning them first so the main statement can stand as a short sentence. All of it stays within verse 18.

records.source: ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει, ἐξ οὗ καὶ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, ὃς μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ δύνασθαι αὐτὸν καὶ ὑποτάξαι αὑτῷ τὰ πάντα.
records.gloss: Of us for the citizenship in heavens exists, from which also a savior we eagerly await, Lord Jesus Christ, \v 21 who will change the body of the humiliation of us conformed to the body of the glory of him according to the working of the to be able him even to subject to himself the all things.
pieces: But we hold our citizenship in heaven, and it is from there that we are eagerly waiting for a Savior, the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}},

who will change these bodies of our humble state and give them the same form as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glorious body, by the working of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power to bring all things under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rule.

L.20: For our citizenship is in [the] heavens, from which also we eagerly await a Savior, [the] Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}},
L.21: who will transform the body of our humiliation [to be] conformed to the body of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory, according to the working by which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is able even to subject all things to {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

R.20: But heaven is the country where we belong as citizens. We are eagerly waiting for a Savior to come from there: the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
R.21: Our bodies are weak and humble now, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will change them to be like {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own body, which is full of glory. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will do it by the power that can bring everything under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rule.

decisions.choice: citizenship: the state to which one belongs, here heaven
alternatives: a home to go to after death
decisions.reason: πολίτευμα is the commonwealth or citizen body a person belongs to. Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), and many in it held Roman citizenship and lived under Rome's law far from Rome (compare Acts 16:21). Believers belong to a state whose seat is in heaven and live by its ways where they are; Paul used the related verb in 1:27. The point is not leaving earth but where their allegiance lies and whom they await from there.

decisions.choice: Savior and Lord: titles Rome also gave its emperors
decisions.reason: In Paul's day the emperor was honored as savior and lord. For citizens of heaven those titles belong to Jesus, who will come from there.

decisions.choice: wait eagerly, with expectation
decisions.reason: ἀπεκδέχομαι is the word Paul uses for waiting for the return of Christ and the redemption of the body (Romans 8:19, 23; 1 Corinthians 1:7).

decisions.choice: the body in its present lowly state: weak and subject to death
decisions.reason: ταπείνωσις is lowliness, not wickedness. It echoes 2:8, where Christ "humbled himself": he shared our lowly state, and he will lift our bodies into his.

decisions.choice: transformed to share the form of his body: the pattern of 2:6-11
decisions.reason: σύμμορφος, "of the same form", echoes 3:10 (being shaped to his death) and the "form" of 2:6-7. The one who took a servant's form and was raised to glory will give his people bodies like his own (compare 1 Corinthians 15:42-53).

decisions.choice: glory: the radiant splendor of God's presence, here in Christ's risen body
decisions.reason: δόξα is God's own shining greatness. "The body of his glory" is Christ's risen body, which shares that splendor.

decisions.choice: the power to subject all things: an echo of Psalm 8:7
decisions.reason: Psalm 8:7 says God put all things under the feet of the son of man, and Paul applies it to Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:27-28. The same power that will rule everything will transform the bodies of believers.

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}
decisions.reason: Pronouns for Christ follow the reader's setting.

decisions.choice: we hold our citizenship (B); the country where we belong as citizens (R)
decisions.reason: Citizenship is the image the Philippians knew from Rome; both levels keep it, as 1:27 does with "live as citizens".

decisions.choice: these bodies of our humble state (B); weak and humble (R)
decisions.reason: "Vile" now means disgusting, which the Greek does not say. Readable says what lowliness means for the body.
